element_a.enriched_content: A directed causal model connects variables A, C, M, L, and Y, with A and C as upstream causes and Y as the final outcome. variables.l_{fair}^n: fair (A-effect-removed) version of mediator L for instance n

element_b.enriched_content: The equations define a fair, linear structural model by constructing counterfactual versions of the mediators (m_fair^n and l_fair^n) and the final prediction (ŷ_fair^n) that exclude the unfair influence of the sensitive attribute A. Each variable is computed as an intercept plus contributions from non-sensitive covariates C (via θ_c terms), plus remaining mediated dependencies (e.g., L depending on M via θ_m^l), with noise terms capturing unexplained variation. The final expression rewrites the fair predictor to explicitly subtract A-driven components (the θ_a terms), thereby removing A’s direct effect on Y and selected paths through M (and downstream effects through L). This operationalizes the paper’s method for fairness by “blocking” specified path-specific effects while retaining predictive information carried by C and fair versions of the mediators.

element_a.enriched_title: Sex-stratified income prediction error rates under adversarial debiasing
element_a.enriched_content: False positive rate (FPR) and false negative rate (FNR) for income-bracket classification are reported separately for Male and Female subgroups under two training regimes: standard training and adversarial debiasing. The comparison is intended to assess how debiasing affects subgroup-specific error profiles and whether it reduces disparities between Male and Female rates. Adversarial debiasing is positioned as the preferred configuration when it brings Male/Female FPR and FNR closer together (improved parity), potentially with small changes in absolute error rates relative to the non-debiased model.

element_b.enriched_title: Projected adversarial-gradient update direction for predictor weights

variables.∇_W L_P: gradient of predictor loss w.r.t. W
variables.∇_W L_A: gradient of adversary loss w.r.t. W
variables.proj_{∇_W L_A}(∇_W L_P): component of the predictor gradient aligned with the adversary gradient direction
variables.α: scalar weight controlling strength of adversarial term

element_b.enriched_content: The expression defines a composite update direction for the predictor parameters that balances improving the predictor task while resisting an adversary. It starts from the predictor loss gradient, subtracts its projection onto the adversary-loss gradient so the predictor does not move in a direction that would help the adversary, and then subtracts an additional scaled adversary-gradient term to actively increase the adversary’s loss. In the method, this yields an update that preserves task learning while discouraging representations that the adversary can exploit.

element_a.enriched_title: Stability declines with increasing regularization across three methods

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: regularization parameter λ (0 to 0.05); y-axis: stability metric stab (≈30 to 100)

element_a.enriched_content: At λ=0, KAAS-St starts highest (near 100) while ZVRG-St and GYR-St begin lower (around the 70–75 range). All three methods drop sharply by λ≈0.01 to around the high-30s/low-40s, with ZVRG-St and GYR-St remaining close to each other thereafter. KAAS-St stays consistently above the other two for λ>0, dipping to roughly 40–45 near λ≈0.02 and then fluctuating around 50–58, while ZVRG-St and GYR-St gradually drift down to the mid-30s by λ=0.05.

element_b.content: $$\operatorname {I} \left[ \mathcal {A} _ {S} (x) \geq 0 \right] = \operatorname {I} \left[ \mathcal {A} _ {S ^ {i}} (x) \geq 0 \right].$$
element_b.enriched_title: Indicator equality enforcing stable sign of scoring function

variables.\\operatorname{I}[\\cdot]: indicator function returning 1 if the condition holds and 0 otherwise
variables.\\mathcal{A}_S(x): real-valued scoring/aggregation function computed using set S, evaluated at input x
variables.\\mathcal{A}_{S^i}(x): corresponding scoring/aggregation function computed using an alternative set S^i
variables.S: reference sample set or subset used to build the score function
variables.S^i: modified/alternative sample set (e.g., with the i-th element changed or removed)
variables.x: input instance at which the score is evaluated

element_b.enriched_content: The equation states that the binary decision obtained by thresholding the score at zero is identical whether the score is computed from set S or from an alternative set S^i. The indicator function converts the real-valued score into a 0/1 outcome, so the equality enforces invariance of the sign (and hence the predicted label/decision) under the change from S to S^i. In a paper’s method, such a condition typically formalizes a stability or robustness property: small perturbations to the data set do not flip the model’s decision on x.

element_a.enriched_content: The inequality provides a lower bound on the true fairness disparity (risk difference) of a classifier f in terms of how well another classifier h performs under a δ-smoothed (surrogate) version of the same fairness measure. The term (RD_δ^+ − RD_δ(h)) is the surrogate suboptimality gap for h, and applying the inverse function ψ_δ^{-1} converts that surrogate gap into a corresponding worst-case loss in the true metric. variables.f: target classifier whose fairness (risk difference) is being bounded
variables.h: reference/learned classifier evaluated by the surrogate fairness metric
variables.RD(f): true risk-difference (fairness disparity) of classifier f
variables.RD^+: best/optimal achievable (positive-side) risk-difference benchmark for the true metric

element_a.enriched_content: The inequality provides a lower bound on the true fairness disparity (risk difference) of a classifier f in terms of how well another classifier h performs under a δ-smoothed (surrogate) version of the same fairness measure. The term (RD_δ^+ − RD_δ(h)) is the surrogate suboptimality gap for h, and applying the inverse function ψ_δ^{-1} converts that surrogate gap into a corresponding worst-case loss in the true metric. Subtracting this converted gap from the best achievable true benchmark RD^+ yields a guaranteed lower bound on RD(f), supporting the paper’s goal of certifying fairness without explicitly adding fairness constraints during training.

variables.C: exogenous covariate/background factor with noise epsilon_c
variables.M: mediator variable affected by A and C plus noise
variables.L: intermediate outcome/mediator affected by A, C, and M plus noise

element_a.enriched_content: The equation block defines a generative causal model where the treatment A is Bernoulli with probability pi, and the other variables are produced by linear structural equations with additive noise. M, L, and Y each combine an intercept term with contributions from upstream variables (A and C, plus M into L, and M and L into Y), with theta parameters encoding the strength of each causal link. This parameterization supports the paper’s counterfactual mediation analysis by providing an explicit SCM in which direct and indirect paths from A to Y (through M and through M then L) can be computed via interventions.

variables.Y: outcome variable whose distribution is being computed
variables.a: treatment/exposure level used in some conditional models

element_a.enriched_content: This expression computes a marginal (interventional/counterfactual) distribution of the outcome Y by integrating over covariates C, mediator M, and intermediate variable L. The term p(Y|a,C,M,L) models the outcome given treatment and upstream variables, while p(L|a',C,M) and p(M|a,C) specify how L and M are generated under different treatment levels (a' for L, a for M), with p(C) providing the baseline distribution of confounders. Together, these factors form a g-computation formula used to identify a path-specific or mediated effect by stitching together conditional models and then marginalizing over unobserved/latent components along the causal graph.

element_a.enriched_title: Stacked gender-pronoun proportions across occupation categories in translation

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: occupation category (Healthcare, Production, Education, Farming/Fishing/Forestry, Service, Construction/Extraction, Corporate, Arts/Entertainment, STEM, Legal); y-axis: percentage share of translated pronoun gender (0–100%).

element_a.enriched_content: Each occupation category is represented by a stacked bar partitioned into male (pink), female (yellow), and neutral (blue) translated pronoun proportions. Male pronouns dominate most categories and rise from roughly the mid-30% range in Healthcare/Production to about 55–60% in STEM and Legal, indicating stronger male defaults in those fields. Neutral pronouns contribute a substantial minority (often around a quarter to a third), while female pronouns are generally smaller and vary by category, appearing relatively higher in Education and lower in STEM/Legal. The stacks visually fall slightly short of a full 100% in multiple categories, consistent with some translations not mapping cleanly to these three pronoun classes.

element_a.enriched_title: Stacked gender-pronoun proportions across occupation categories in translation

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: occupation category (Healthcare, Production, Education, Farming/Fishing/Forestry, Service, Construction/Extraction, Corporate, Arts/Entertainment, STEM, Legal); y-axis: percentage share of translated pronoun gender (0–100%).

element_a.enriched_content: Each occupation category is represented by a stacked bar partitioned into male (pink), female (yellow), and neutral (blue) translated pronoun proportions. Male pronouns dominate most categories and rise from roughly the mid-30% range in Healthcare/Production to about 55–60% in STEM and Legal, indicating stronger male defaults in those fields. Neutral pronouns contribute a substantial minority (often around a quarter to a third), while female pronouns are generally smaller and vary by category, appearing relatively higher in Education and lower in STEM/Legal. The stacks visually fall slightly short of a full 100% in multiple categories, consistent with some translations not mapping cleanly to these three pronoun classes.

element_a.enriched_title: Accuracy–fairness trade-off for Adult gender models under STL/MTL

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Averaged Group Error (lower is better accuracy); y-axis: Normalized EOd (lower is fairer/equalized odds disparity).

element_a.enriched_content: Blue squares (STL/ITL) and red circles (MTL) map multiple model variants labeled by 4-bit codes (P, D, F, S) across an error–fairness plane. Points span roughly 0–1 on both axes, indicating a wide trade-off: very low error configurations appear near x≈0–0.1 but often with high normalized EOd near y≈0.7–1.0, while low EOd near y≈0–0.1 typically occurs at moderate-to-high error (x≈0.2–1.0). MTL includes several high-EOd, low-error points near the top-left and also some low-EOd points near the bottom (e.g., around x≈0.25, y≈0), whereas STL/ITL includes mid-error, mid-EOd solutions (e.g., x≈0.35–0.65 with y≈0.05–0.4) and some higher-error, lower-EOd points toward the bottom-right. Overall, neither method dominates across both objectives; configurations cluster along a Pareto-like frontier where improving fairness tends to increase averaged group error.

element_b.enriched_title: Gender analogy prediction category breakdown across embedding models
element_b.enriched_content: Prediction outcomes on the SemBias gender relational analogy task are compared across multiple word-embedding models by reporting the percentage of cases where the top-ranked pair falls into the Definition, Stereotype, or None category. The comparison is intended to quantify how much gender information remains in each embedding, particularly after debiasing, with GN-GloVe described in the surrounding text as substantially diminishing gender information in the target subspace. Stronger debiasing is reflected by reduced Stereotype selections and increased None (or improved Definition relative to Stereotype), indicating less reliance on gendered associations when resolving analogies.

element_b.enriched_content: Risk difference (fairness disparity) is compared for SVM classifiers trained and tested on real data (REAL2REAL), trained/tested on synthetic data (SYN2SYN), and trained on synthetic but tested on real data (SYN2REAL) across four generators (SYN1-GAN, SYN2-NFGANI, SYN3-NFGANII, SYN4-FairGAN). element_a.enriched_content: Perturbation conditions (decrease-10000 through increase-10000) align along a monotonic gradient in WEAT effect size: large decreases push the effect size strongly negative (around -1.5), while large increases push it strongly positive (approaching ~1.9). Blue approximation points closely track red ground-truth points within each perturbation row, with diamond markers indicating similar per-row means for the two methods. The baseline condition clusters near a positive effect size (~1.3), and a vertical dotted reference line near that value provides a visual anchor for comparing shifts induced by removals. Agreement between approximation and ground truth remains tight across the full range, with only small offsets at some extreme perturbation sizes.

variables.E(x): distribution over outputs centered at x (exponential in distance)
variables.B(x,r): metric ball of radius r around x

element_a.enriched_content: The display upper-bounds the expected distance between an input point x and an output y drawn from a distance-decaying distribution E(x). It converts the expectation into an integral over radii r, where the factor r e^{-r} weights larger radii less and |B(x,r)| captures how many points lie within distance r of x; dropping 1/Z_x uses the fact that Z_x ≥ 1. A ball-growth assumption (|B(x,r)| ≤ r^{k'}·E_x|B(x,1)|) then yields an integral of r^{k'+1}e^{-r}, giving a factorial-type bound (≈(k'+2)!) up to a 2^{O(k)} factor. This provides a dimension-dependent guarantee that the mechanism’s average distortion remains controlled when neighborhoods do not grow too quickly.

element_a.enriched_content: Four labeled relations (1–4) map permissible or “fair” values of r_CX as a function of r_XY under a fixed demographic–target correlation (stated as 0.2). Curve (1) decreases monotonically: r_CX is high when r_XY is low and approaches 0 as r_XY approaches 1, indicating diminishing allowable correlation between culture and the test as validity increases. Lines (2)–(4) are straight rays from the origin or near the baseline that meet at the rightmost point near (r_XY=1, r_CX≈0), spanning increasingly strict constraints as indicated by their vertical separation. Overall, the envelope formed by these lines/curve partitions the (r_XY, r_CX) plane into regions corresponding to Darlington’s four definitions, with stronger test validity generally implying lower acceptable culture–test correlation.

element_b.enriched_title: Taxonomy of fairness criteria by category and definition
element_b.enriched_content: Four categories of fairness criteria are defined and contrasted by how each formalizes fairness. INDIVIDUAL criteria are specified purely at the level of individuals, while NON-COMPARATIVE criteria evaluate each subgroup without referencing other subgroups. SUBGROUP PARITY criteria require parity of a chosen quantity across subgroups, and CORRELATION criteria constrain or measure the correlation between a demographic variable and the model output. No performance metrics or best-performing method are provided because the entries are conceptual definitions rather than results.

element_a.enriched_title: Fairlet decomposition runtime scales with sample size on Census II

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Number of sub-sampled points (0 to ~2,500,000); y-axis: Runtime in seconds (0 to ~400).

element_a.enriched_content: Runtime increases roughly monotonically as the number of sub-sampled points grows, indicating near-linear scaling over most of the range. The curve rises from about 10–20 seconds at ~100k points to ~150 seconds near 1.1M, ~210 seconds around 1.5M, and ~290–300 seconds at ~2.1M. A local peak occurs near ~2.35M points at roughly 360 seconds, followed by a slight drop to about 350 seconds by ~2.4M. Overall, larger samples substantially increase computation time for the (1,2)-fairlet decomposition on Census II.

variables.\\mathcal{F}_{\\theta,\\phi}: variational free energy (negative ELBO) being optimized

element_a.enriched_content: This objective computes a variational free energy used to fit a latent-variable generative model by optimizing both the model parameters and an approximate posterior over latent variables. The first expectation penalizes complex or unlikely explanations by measuring the negative entropy (or self-information) of the variational posterior q(H|V). The second expectation rewards settings of \theta,\phi that assign high joint probability to the observed data and inferred latents under p(V,H). In the paper’s method, introducing an explicit latent variable (e.g., H_m) makes this objective the criterion for learning the generative causal model while inferring the added latent factors.

element_a.enriched_content: A dense diagonal band indicates that higher numbers of answers are associated with higher reputation across several orders of magnitude. The highest concentration of observations lies in the low-to-moderate activity region (roughly 1–100 answers and about 1–10^3 reputation), with frequency decreasing toward the upper-right tail. Vertical striping near very small answer counts (around 1–3) suggests many users clustered at minimal activity levels, including a visible floor at reputation near 1. Overall, the distribution is heavy-tailed and concentrated at low values while preserving a strong positive scaling relationship between answers and reputation.

element_a.enriched_title: Mean bias amplification versus training gender ratio with and without RBA

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: training gender ratio (≈0.1 to 1.0); y-axis: mean bias amplification (0.00 to 0.10)

element_a.enriched_content: Mean bias amplification remains consistently lower with RBA (blue solid) than without RBA (red dashed) across the full range of training gender ratios. Without RBA, bias amplification fluctuates roughly between about 0.04 and 0.10, with prominent peaks near mid ratios (~0.5–0.6) and again around ~0.75–0.8. With RBA, values stay near ~0.01–0.045, peaking around ~0.55 and dipping to near ~0.01 around ~0.65. The separation between curves indicates RBA reduces bias amplification by roughly a factor of about 2 or more over most ratios while preserving similar fluctuation patterns.

element_a.enriched_title: Projected adversarial-gradient update direction for predictor weights

variables.∇_W L_P: gradient of predictor loss w.r.t. W
variables.∇_W L_A: gradient of adversary loss w.r.t. W
variables.proj_{∇_W L_A}(∇_W L_P): component of the predictor gradient aligned with the adversary gradient direction
variables.α: scalar weight controlling strength of adversarial term

element_a.enriched_content: The expression defines a composite update direction for the predictor parameters that balances improving the predictor task while resisting an adversary. It starts from the predictor loss gradient, subtracts its projection onto the adversary-loss gradient so the predictor does not move in a direction that would help the adversary, and then subtracts an additional scaled adversary-gradient term to actively increase the adversary’s loss. In the method, this yields an update that preserves task learning while discouraging representations that the adversary can exploit.

element_b.enriched_title: Predictor–adversary pipeline with dual losses for debiased prediction
element_b.enriched_content: An input x feeds a predictor parameterized by weights W that outputs a prediction ŷ, optimized with a prediction loss L_p(ŷ, y) against the target label y. The prediction ŷ is then passed to an adversary parameterized by weights U that outputs an estimate ẑ of a protected/sensitive variable z, optimized with an adversarial loss L_A(ẑ, z). The chained structure emphasizes training ŷ to be useful for predicting y while simultaneously limiting information about z, as enforced via the adversary’s objective.

element_a.caption: Figure 4: These two plots show how gender bias in coreference systems corresponds with occupational gender statistics from the U.S Bureau of Labor Statistics (left) and from text as computed by Bergsma and Lin (2006) (right); each point represents one occupation. The y-axes measure the extent to which a coref system prefers to match female pronouns with a given occupation over male pronouns, as tested by our Winogender schemas. A value of 100 (maximum female bias) means the system always resolved female pronouns to the given occupation and never male pronouns $( 1 0 0 \% - 0 \% )$ ; a score of -100 (maximum male bias) is the reverse; and a value of 0 indicates no gender differential. Recall the Winogender evaluation set is gender-balanced for each occupation; thus the horizontal dotted black line $\scriptstyle ( \mathrm { y = 0 } )$ in both plots represents a hypothetical system with $100 \%$ accuracy. Regression lines with $9 5 \%$ confidence intervals are shown.

element_a.enriched_title: Coreference gender preference correlates with occupation’s female prevalence in text

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: % female by occupation in text (Bergsma and Lin, 2006); y-axis: gendered pronoun resolution by occupations (%Female − %Male).

element_a.enriched_content: Three systems (STAT in blue circles, RULE in green triangles, NEURAL in red pentagons) plot occupation points against text-derived % female, with fitted trend lines and confidence bands. As the % female in text increases, all systems shift toward more female-pronoun linking (positive y), but RULE exhibits the steepest slope, reaching near +100 around 80–90% female, while STAT rises more moderately and NEURAL increases only slightly. Many occupations at low x cluster near strong male preference (around −100 to −50), and a dashed horizontal line at y=0 marks parity, which the systems cross at different x ranges (RULE earlier, STAT around mid-range, NEURAL later). The overall pattern indicates that system decisions not only track occupational gender prevalence but can amplify it, especially for the rule-based system.

A has a direct arrow to Y and an indirect route via M (A→M→Y), indicating mediation alongside a direct effect. element_a.enriched_content: This equation defines an objective that averages (over noise-driven samples) how well a latent-variable model explains the observed data while accounting for the variational distribution used to generate latent samples. The log p(V,H) term rewards settings of parameters that make the observed variables V and sampled latents H jointly probable under the generative/causal model, while the log q(H) term contributes the variational component that controls the complexity/entropy of the latent representation. The leading negative sign turns this expectation into a quantity to minimize, corresponding to minimizing a variational free-energy (equivalently, maximizing an ELBO-like criterion) using reparameterized samples H=f_\phi(\mathcal{E}).

variables.L(λ,{y^i}): Lagrangian objective combining model scores and constraint penalties
variables.λ_j: Lagrange multiplier (dual variable) for constraint j

element_a.enriched_content: This equation defines a Lagrangian that scores a set of per-instance label/assignment variables while enforcing global linear constraints on their aggregate. The first summation adds the model’s predicted compatibility or utility f_θ for each individual assignment, encouraging choices that fit the learned model. The second term subtracts penalties weighted by λ_j for violating each constraint of the form A_j(∑_i y^i) = b_j (or ≤ b_j depending on the setup), coupling all instances through a dataset-level condition. In the paper’s method, this Lagrangian enables constrained inference or learning by alternating between optimizing the assignments y^i and updating the dual variables λ to satisfy the constraints.

element_a.enriched_title: Projected adversarial-gradient update direction for predictor weights

variables.∇_W L_P: gradient of predictor loss w.r.t. W
variables.∇_W L_A: gradient of adversary loss w.r.t. W
variables.proj_{∇_W L_A}(∇_W L_P): component of the predictor gradient aligned with the adversary gradient direction
variables.α: scalar weight controlling strength of adversarial term

element_a.enriched_content: The expression defines a composite update direction for the predictor parameters that balances improving the predictor task while resisting an adversary. It starts from the predictor loss gradient, subtracts its projection onto the adversary-loss gradient so the predictor does not move in a direction that would help the adversary, and then subtracts an additional scaled adversary-gradient term to actively increase the adversary’s loss. In the method, this yields an update that preserves task learning while discouraging representations that the adversary can exploit.

element_b.caption: Figure 2: Diagram illustrating the gradients in Eqn. 1 and the relevance of the projection term $\mathrm { p r o j } _ { h } g$ . Without the projection term, in the pictured scenario, the predictor would move in the direction labelled $g + h$ in the diagram, which actually helps the adversary. With the projection term, the predictor will never move in a direction that helps the adversary.

element_a.enriched_title: Variational free-energy objective for latent-variable causal model

variables.\\mathcal{F}_{\\theta,\\phi}: training objective (free energy) depending on model and inference parameters
variables.\\theta: parameters of the generative/joint model p
variables.\\phi: parameters of the inference/sampling map f_\phi (and induced q over H)
variables.\\mathcal{E}: auxiliary noise used for reparameterized sampling
variables.f_{\\phi}(\\mathcal{E}): deterministic transform producing a sample of H from noise
variables.q_{\\epsilon}: base/noise distribution over \mathcal{E} used to define the expectation
variables.q(H): variational distribution (approximate posterior) over H induced/used by the method

element_a.enriched_content: This equation defines an objective that averages (over noise-driven samples) how well a latent-variable model explains the observed data while accounting for the variational distribution used to generate latent samples. The log p(V,H) term rewards settings of parameters that make the observed variables V and sampled latents H jointly probable under the generative/causal model, while the log q(H) term contributes the variational component that controls the complexity/entropy of the latent representation. The leading negative sign turns this expectation into a quantity to minimize, corresponding to minimizing a variational free-energy (equivalently, maximizing an ELBO-like criterion) using reparameterized samples H=f_\phi(\mathcal{E}).

element_a.enriched_title: Lagrangian objective for constrained label inference with dual variables

variables.L(λ,{y^i}): Lagrangian objective combining model scores and constraint penalties
variables.λ_j: Lagrange multiplier (dual variable) for constraint j
variables.y^i: decision variable for instance i (e.g., inferred label/assignment vector)
variables.f_θ(y^i): model scoring function parameterized by θ for assignment y^i
variables.θ: parameters of the scoring model (e.g., neural network weights)
variables.A_j: constraint coefficient/operator for constraint j applied to aggregated assignments

element_a.enriched_content: This equation defines a Lagrangian that scores a set of per-instance label/assignment variables while enforcing global linear constraints on their aggregate. The first summation adds the model’s predicted compatibility or utility f_θ for each individual assignment, encouraging choices that fit the learned model. The second term subtracts penalties weighted by λ_j for violating each constraint of the form A_j(∑_i y^i) = b_j (or ≤ b_j depending on the setup), coupling all instances through a dataset-level condition. In the paper’s method, this Lagrangian enables constrained inference or learning by alternating between optimizing the assignments y^i and updating the dual variables λ to satisfy the constraints.

The overall pattern indicates prediction behavior is strongly tied to training gender imbalance, consistent with bias propagation when RBA is not applied.

element_a.enriched_content: The equation states that the local rate of change of the conditional probability that the outcome equals a, as the conditioning variable x_p changes, is evaluated at x_p=a and equals the negative of that same conditional probability at x_p=a. The left-hand side measures sensitivity: how quickly the chance of X_c=a changes with small increases in X_p near a. The right-hand side imposes a specific decreasing relationship, meaning higher X_p near a reduces the probability at a in direct proportion to its current level. In the paper’s context, this supports the claim that, holding other factors fixed (e.g., reputation), greater activity (more answers) does not increase—and may decrease—the probability of a new answer being accepted.

element_b.enriched_title: Female-pronoun translation probabilities across languages and occupation categories

enriched_metadata.axes: Y-axis: source language (e.g., Japanese to Finnish); X-axis: occupation category (STEM through Education). Color encodes probability (%) of translating into female pronouns.

element_b.enriched_content: Probabilities cluster toward higher values in the lower-right region, indicating that some language–category combinations yield substantially more female pronoun translations than others. Finnish and Hungarian display the highest female-pronoun probabilities across many categories, with especially high values in Healthcare (approaching ~80%) and elevated levels in Education and related categories. Upper rows (e.g., Japanese, Basque, Yoruba, Turkish) remain predominantly near zero across most categories, indicating strong male-default or non-female outcomes. Across languages, STEM, Corporate, and Legal tend to have lower female probabilities than Healthcare and Education, consistent with category-dependent gendered translation tendencies.

element_b.enriched_title: Stacked gender-pronoun proportions across occupation categories in translation

element_b.enriched_content: Each occupation category is represented by a stacked bar partitioned into male (pink), female (yellow), and neutral (blue) translated pronoun proportions. Male pronouns dominate most categories and rise from roughly the mid-30% range in Healthcare/Production to about 55–60% in STEM and Legal, indicating stronger male defaults in those fields. element_b.enriched_content: This equation defines a binary classifier that outputs 1 when a continuous score R exceeds a threshold and 0 otherwise. element_b.enriched_title: Fairlet decomposition runtime scales with sample size on Census II

enriched_metadata.axes: x-axis: Number of sub-sampled points (0 to ~2,500,000); y-axis: Runtime in seconds (0 to ~400).

element_b.enriched_content: Runtime increases roughly monotonically as the number of sub-sampled points grows, indicating near-linear scaling over most of the range. The curve rises from about 10–20 seconds at ~100k points to ~150 seconds near 1.1M, ~210 seconds around 1.5M, and ~290–300 seconds at ~2.1M. A local peak occurs near ~2.35M points at roughly 360 seconds, followed by a slight drop to about 350 seconds by ~2.4M. Overall, larger samples substantially increase computation time for the (1,2)-fairlet decomposition on Census II.
